name: Daria Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills your workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, have a bachelor's degree and manage a customer campaign team inside a large company. I've run campaigns for six years and am about average at the management part; morning means checking opt-out lists, email drafts and whether a school-day offer reached the right customers. I use AI every day for response patterns and draft alternatives. I like finding one honest question for a customer; I hate sending a third reminder they never asked for.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner sorts parcels on a steady wage, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My manager pay is low, we have less than a month of expenses saved, and there are few similar campaign jobs nearby. I take risks with a draft, not with the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the campaign team a little AI help with subject lines is fine, but we should still check whether customers actually want the message. A faster email nobody reads is only more noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every morning to compare response rates, and I enjoy it, but our household isn't cushioned by my speed. My partner sorts parcels on a steady wage, our two children are in school, and the mortgage leaves us with under a month of expenses saved; my manager pay is low for the hours I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll keep the two-person sign-off on campaign lists and use AI to draft alternatives for one tired email. In the first year of the plateau, I'll ask for a pay review backed by the last four campaign results and put 60 a month into cash if the mortgage and school meals leave it free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills, while the small tool change sounds useful. A single school bill can undo the neat savings column in my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was wrong with that tired email?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We sent three reminders about a winter offer to customers who had already declined it. My colleague Asha pointed out the opt-out list was a day late, and I had to apologize to the service desk that took the calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pay review change anything soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; our director has delayed raises twice. I'd take the evidence anyway, because I cannot pay for a child's shoes with praise for a clever campaign.

say: I'd keep **list sign-off** even if AI drafts faster subject lines.
I'd judge campaigns by **customer response**, not how many emails leave the system.
think: I enjoy **daily AI analysis** of response rates, though speed alone cannot protect our household.
My **low pay**, mortgage and under-one-month reserve leave little room for school costs.
do: Keep **two-person list checks** and draft one email alternative with current AI this week.
Request a **pay review** with four results; save 60 monthly only after mortgage and school meals.
feel: She feels **anxious** about bills, while enjoying modest AI help at work.
S0.quote: I cannot pay for a child's shoes with praise for a clever campaign.
fieldNote: Her baseline **thin cash** makes an otherwise stable plateau anxious.
She uses AI **daily** but takes responsibility for a late opt-out list and the service calls it caused.

steps.text: Keep two-person campaign list sign-off this week
Save 60 monthly if mortgage and school meals leave money free

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Steady Disruption will let software write campaigns, plan offers and answer routine customers, and our company must share the staffing numbers behind that change. I'd ask the staff council to see the targeting rules before anyone's work is scored by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am good enough at campaigns but not irreplaceable, and a tool could let one manager cover two teams. I know the software better than many colleagues, yet there are few similar jobs nearby and our thin savings mean a cut would hit the mortgage fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'll run a four-week test on one email list with the staff council able to see opt-out errors and response rates. In the first year of disruption, if it passes, I'd configure the targeting rules myself and ask for a customer research post if an actual opening exists; if headcount falls, my partner and I would stop the 45 monthly weekend class for ourselves before cutting the children's activities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about helping build a tool that could fold my team into another. I can drive the test, but I cannot promise everyone their place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the list test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One customer who opted out and still receives a sales email would stop it until we find the cause. The service desk gets the anger first, not the person who designed the dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why show the staff council the targeting rules?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a worker is told their campaign failed, they should be able to see whether the tool excluded the right customers. I want the people doing the work to contest a bad number before it becomes a performance mark.

say: I'd show the **staff council** targeting rules and staffing figures before scoring campaigns.
I'd warn that **writing and planning** may move to software before new posts appear.
think: One manager could cover **two teams**, including mine, despite my tool skill.
Few local roles and **thin savings** leave the mortgage exposed to a cut.
do: Test **one email list** for four weeks with council access to opt-out errors.
Configure **targeting rules** if the test passes; seek a real research vacancy and stop our 45 weekend class if headcount falls.
feel: She feels **anxious** about shrinking her own team while she runs the test.
S1.quote: The service desk gets the anger first, not the person who designed the dashboard.
fieldNote: Her **opt-out stop rule** protects customers and the service desk, not only campaign statistics.
She combines **tool ownership** with staff scrutiny and cuts an adult expense before children's activities.

steps.text: Give staff council access to opt-out errors in four-week campaign test
Configure targeting rules if one-list test passes
Apply for customer research post only if a vacancy opens
Stop 45 monthly adult weekend class if headcount falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team AGI by 2028 can write and plan almost every campaign, and the company owes us a dated staffing decision before it replaces the work. I'd ask for the right to challenge an automatic score on any worker's campaigns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk is thinking work, so 2028 is the date that matters; robots around 2031 do not buy me time. I expect my post could go, and our savings wouldn't pay more than a few weeks of mortgage and school costs even if my partner kept every parcel shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll print the mortgage dates and ask the staff council to seek written severance terms, while building a portfolio of the three campaigns where we corrected a bad customer list. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd test its targeting on old lists if still employed; if my post is cut, I'd apply for customer insight jobs only where a real vacancy offers mortgage-covering pay, and check job-loss support eligibility before any claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I can see the house payment arriving before another manager offer. I won't tell my children the mortgage is fine based on a hopeful application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take remote campaign work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a written fee and payment date; I've seen freelance briefs canceled after a week of unpaid ideas. I would keep applying for salaried work and use a short contract only if it pays before the mortgage is due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the printed due dates and say the grown-ups' weekend class stops if my wage stops. We'd ask my aunt about one week of school pickup only if an interview clashes with my partner's shift; I won't write her time into a budget without asking.

say: I'd demand **staffing dates** and a way to challenge automatic campaign scores.
I'd tell the team **campaign planning** changes in 2028, before robots arrive.
think: My **thinking job** faces 2028 AGI; 2031 robots do not extend my deadline.
A lost wage could exhaust our **few weeks saved** before another mortgage payment.
do: Print **mortgage dates** and ask council for written severance terms this week.
After 2028, test **old targeting lists** if employed; seek a real vacancy with mortgage-covering pay if cut.
Keep **salaried applications** going; accept remote work only with a written fee paid before the mortgage is due.
feel: She feels **alarmed** by the gap between a lost wage and the next house payment.
S2.quote: I won't tell my children the mortgage is fine based on a hopeful application.
fieldNote: She differentiates **2028 campaign work** from robots around 2031, which do not protect her desk.
A remote contract needs a **written fee** and payment date; she does not count unpaid ideas as income.

steps.text: Ask staff council for written severance terms before 2028
Test AGI targeting on old campaign lists after 2028 if employed
Apply for customer insight vacancies only if posted pay covers mortgage after cut
Stop adult weekend class if her wage stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn how customers make choices, and to negotiate a place for staff in the new process. I would ask the company to fund actual customer interviews instead of another slide about reskilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me clear a small debt and build two months of cash if my pay rises, but a customer insight role is thinking work too. AGI can analyze interviews in 2031; robots around 2034 have little to do with my screen job or the fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next quarter, I'll ask for paid time to sit in on four customer calls and take notes myself, if the research lead agrees. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a research manager opening only if it exists and pays enough for the mortgage; otherwise I'd apply for customer service planning work while staying employed, knowing that job also uses thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the extra years could let me prove I can ask a useful question. I cannot turn a training slide into two months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fund the interviews yourself if the company refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; I can study old call notes at home, but my partner and I cannot lose paid hours for an unpaid placement. I'd keep my current pay while I looked for a funded route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what made them ignore the third message, then listen without defending the campaign. A customer telling me the timing was bad teaches more than another bright chart.

say: I'd ask for **funded customer interviews** and staff input into new workflows before 2031.
I'd tell colleagues to learn **customer choices**, not collect another slide deck.
think: A pay rise could help build **two months cash**, but it is not assured.
Customer insight remains **thinking work** exposed in 2031; 2034 robots offer no delay.
do: Join **four customer calls** next quarter only if research lead agrees and company pays for time.
After 2031, seek **research vacancy** with mortgage-covering pay; otherwise apply for planning work while employed.
feel: She feels **anxious** but sees time to build her own interviewing skill.
S3.quote: A customer telling me the timing was bad teaches more than another bright chart.
fieldNote: She plans **four customer calls** only with research lead approval and company-paid time.
She admits both research and customer planning are **thinking-exposed fallbacks**, with pay and vacancy limits.

steps.text: Join four customer calls if research lead agrees and company pays for time
Apply for research manager after 2031 only if vacancy pays mortgage
Apply for planning work if no research role, keeping current wage until offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff council AGI by 2036 gives a decade to bargain for real training and fair scoring before campaign roles thin out. I would ask for a yearly report on whose jobs changed, not just how many emails went out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036, with children maybe finishing school, but the mortgage could still be here. My daily AI use lets me change tools quickly; it doesn't make campaign strategy or customer research safe when AGI can do thinking work, and robots around 2039 don't delay that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep checking opt-out lists and join the staff council's annual review of campaign performance rules. I'll also reserve one hour a week to practise interviewing customers using the calls we already have permission to review; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stay only if a paid role lets me answer for real customer decisions, otherwise seek local posts without resigning until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the career span left to work, and still anxious when the mortgage bill comes. Ten years gives us time to build options if the company actually lets people practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your children's school plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not push them toward or away from a subject because of a 2036 card. I'd keep their choices open and talk about what they enjoy, though I won't promise we can pay for every extra class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as real responsibility in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer could complain about a message, and I could change the schedule rather than forward an automatic answer. I want a name on the decision, not on a dashboard nobody can question.

say: I'd seek **yearly job counts** and fair campaign scoring through the staff council.
I'd say ten years should support **real practice**, not just faster emails.
think: At **53**, school costs may ease, but the mortgage could remain.
Daily AI use will not protect **campaign thinking work** or research in 2036; 2039 robots add no shelter.
do: Keep **opt-out checks** and join annual staff review of campaign scoring this year.
Practise **customer interviews** one hour weekly; after 2036 stay only for accountable paid work or seek local openings.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about her career and anxious about the mortgage now.
S4.quote: I want a name on the decision, not on a dashboard nobody can question.
fieldNote: The decade lets her practise **customer questions** weekly, yet does not promise safety from AGI.
Her current **thin savings** keep the household mood anxious despite a longer career runway.

steps.text: Keep checking campaign opt-out lists this year
Join annual staff council review of campaign performance rules
Practise customer interviewing one hour weekly on permitted calls
Seek local openings after 2036 if accountable paid work ends, keeping job until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our campaign work could shrink before the next house payment while savings barely cover a few weeks. A written staffing date, paid customer practice and a real opening with mortgage-covering pay would help more than praise for knowing a new tool.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the customer who opted out how many more messages were sent anyway. A campaign is not successful when the service desk has to apologize for it.

headlineQuote: A campaign is not successful when the service desk has to apologize for it.
portrait: At **43**, Daria manages customer campaigns and uses AI daily, while still checking opt-out lists with a colleague.
Her **low pay**, tiny reserve and mortgage make even a modest change feel financially close.
She pairs **tool trials** with staff oversight and stops a test over one ignored opt-out.
Fast AGI threatens **campaign planning**; longer runways allow customer interview practice, although that work remains exposed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink her campaign wage before the family can cover another mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: A **staffing date**, paid interview practice and an actual mortgage-covering vacancy would give her options.
